title: Case studies: the Hardap Irrigation Scheme, and food shortage in the Sahel

blocks.heading: The case studies
blocks.text: Two required case studies at the scale the syllabus asks for: one agricultural system - the Hardap Irrigation Scheme on the Fish River in southern Namibia - and one region suffering food shortages - the Sahel belt of West Africa.

blocks.heading: Case study: the Hardap Irrigation Scheme
blocks.text: The Hardap Irrigation Scheme lies on the Fish River just south of Mariental in southern Namibia. The Hardap Dam, completed in 1963, holds the river's summer floods, and roughly 1 100 hectares of irrigated land below the dam (approximate figure) grow lucerne (alfalfa) for fodder, along with maize, wheat, vegetables and grapes. The scheme is a commercial agricultural system: its inputs include the dam's water delivered by canal and pump, fertiliser, heavy machinery and a resident workforce; its processes are land preparation, sowing, irrigation through the dry months, weed and pest control, and harvest; and its outputs are fodder, grain, vegetables and grapes sold to dairy and beef farmers and to produce markets, with run-off and crop residues as its waste streams.

blocks.heading: Why Hardap is classified as it is
blocks.text: Each classification earns its place. Commercial: nearly everything the scheme grows is sold for profit, which distinguishes it at a stroke from a family food plot. Intensive: the scheme concentrates high inputs on each hectare - pumped water, fertiliser, machinery and full-time labour - because the area's rainfall, under about 200 millimetres a year, is far too low for dry-land cropping; those inputs buy high yields per hectare, which is the definition of intensive farming. Arable in its crops, and pastoral indirectly, since its lucerne feeds livestock elsewhere. The classification is the analysis: a farm in a dry land must be intensive precisely where water is engineered to be plentiful.

blocks.heading: Case study: food shortages in the Sahel
blocks.text: The Sahel is the dry belt along the southern edge of the Sahara, across countries such as Niger, Mali, Burkina Faso and Chad. Its people farm and herd on thin soils with rain that is low and unreliable - under about 400 millimetres a year in places - and when the rains fail, the region starves: the drought of 1984 brought failed harvests across the belt, and the crisis of 2010-2012, following another drought, left over 18 million people at risk of hunger (approximate figure, 2012). Between the droughts, human pressures build: rapid population growth strains the land, overgrazing and tree clearance degrade it, and conflict - as in Mali in 2012 - drives farmers from their fields.

blocks.heading: Effects and solutions, traced
blocks.text: The shortage's effects run in the chain this topic teaches: harvests fail, grain prices rise, families eat less, and undernutrition follows - measured across the Sahel in the tens of millions of people in bad years; herders move south with their cattle as pastures fail, which strains the regions they enter; and families sell assets to buy food, which deepens poverty after the crisis. The solutions tried show both sides of the balance: grain banks and reserves run by cooperatives bridge bad seasons; tree-planting and terracing hold soil and water on the land; improved seed and small-scale irrigation raise yields; and food aid flows in the worst years - saving lives, but as cheap grain it can undercut the local growers the region needs next season. Judged against scale, cost and reliability, the Sahel's solutions work best together: the grain bank bridges the crisis while the land work slowly rebuilds the base.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Both case studies draw on the water sources of topic 3.6 - the Fish River's floods and the Sahel's rains - and both sit inside the development story of topic 3.1: commercial irrigation for markets on one side, subsistence farming under pressure on the other. The Sahel's land degradation feeds the environmental risks of topic 3.7.
